contraindications: If silently saying 'Thinking' is not helpful, discontinue its use
original_extraction.evidence_text:
I’ve designed the above brief exercises for busy people who say they ‘don’t have enough time in the
day’ to do formal defusion practice. However, “not enough time” is just another story. So here”s a
challenge for you: if you really want to get good at this, then as well as doing all those brief
exercises, put aside five minutes twice a day to practise focusing on your breath. For example, you
may do five minutes first thing in the morning and five minutes during your lunchbreak. During
these times, keep your attention totally on your breath, while letting your thoughts come and go in
the background; and each time you notice your attention has wandered, gently bring 1t back. Also, 1f
you haven't already tried it, then try silently saying to yourself, “Thinking”, whenever a thought or
image appears. Some people find this very helpful as a way of acknowledging the thinking process
without getting caught up in it. (However, if you don’t find it helpful, then don’t bother with it.)

---

Defusion skills are essential for escaping the happiness trap. If you can see your thoughts for what
they are—just words—and let them come and go without focusing on them, then you can put your
time and energy into more important things, such as taking action to create the life you want. Your
mind will never stop telling you unpleasant stories (at least, not for long)—that’s just what minds
do. So let’s be realistic. The fact is, you will get hooked up and reeled in by these stories again and
again.

---

The good news is, you can make dramatic improvements. You can learn to get hooked much less
often. You can learn to recognise much faster when you have been hooked, and you can learn to get
much better at unhooking yourself! All these abilities will help to keep you out of the happiness
trap.
generation_rules: Set aside two five-minute periods daily to focus on breath
Gently bring attention back when it wanders
Optionally use the word 'Thinking' silently when thoughts arise
pause_rules: Pause to notice the presence of thoughts without engaging
Pause briefly when attention shifts before redirecting focus
original_extraction.psychological_function: Enhancing awareness of the thinking process, increasing ability to notice when attention has wandered, and improving capacity to gently redirect focus back to the present moment.
repetition_rules: Repeatedly notice when attention has wandered and bring it back to breath
Silently label thoughts as 'Thinking' each time they appear (optional)
symbolic_elements: silently saying 'Thinking' to acknowledge thoughts without engagement
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: Developing defusion skills to observe thoughts as mere words and reduce attachment to them, thereby escaping the happiness trap and enabling focus on meaningful actions.
voice_rules: Use gentle, non-judgmental tone when redirecting attention
Encourage self-compassion when noticing mind wandering
